newsitem.title: CHILE: China declares Chile free of the fruit fly.
newsitem.headline: China declares Chile free of the fruit fly.

text.p: China has declared Chile free of the Mediterranean fruit fly, lifting a barrier to most varieties of fresh fruit, one of Chile's top exports, the foreign ministry said Thursday.

Chinese Vice Premier Li Lanqing told Chilean authorities that his government had accepted Chilean assurances that it had eradicated the fruit fly, a tiny insect which degrades fruit pulp by laying its eggs in it and which first appeared in Chile in the early 1960s.

"He informed us that the Chinese government has made the decision to declare Chile free of the Mediterranean fruit fly, insofar as its purchases of Chilean kiwis, apples and grapes from some regions are concerned," said acting Foreign Minister Mariano Fernandez.
But he said China's restrictions on Chilean exports because of the fly infestation would stay in effect on grapes from some regions of Chile, at least temporarily.
Lanqing arrived Tuesday in Santiago from Cuba as part of a Latin American tour also including Colombia, Brazil and Argentina and focusing on economic and trade issues.
Chilean fruit exports stand at about $1.4 billion a year, meaning it vies with paper pulp as Chile's second-largest export after copper.
Lanqing reiterated China's long-standing interest in investing in Chilean copper mining, said Fernandez.

"They're very interested in mining, particularly in the copper sector," he said. "President (Eduardo) Frei insisted that he be concrete on the issue of Chinese investments in copper, and that we lend all assistance so that (investments) in copper can move ahead."
He gave no details. Despite about two years of high-level contacts, the two countries have yet to reach an agreement for Chinese investment in a major Chilean copper mining project.

Fernandez said total trade between the two nations had risen to $860 million last year from $430 million in 1994, with a surplus of about $150 million in China's favor although Chile was not worried about the gap.
"The government isn't overly concerned if we have a surplus or a deficit with that country. The important thing is that trade not lose its dynamism, that growth rates are maintained," he said.

"Our stand was to ask the Chinese government to collaborate more with us on quotas for (Chilean) products, on customs duty reductions and also on the lifting of some sanitary restrictions (on exports from Chile). The response was quite positive," said Fernandez.

He said they also discussed China's human rights situation. Fernandez said he told him Chile will keep up its concern permanently on the issue "and not just argue with them only the eve of meetings of the (U.N.) human rights commission."
